input: The rate constant $k$ of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures, and the two values state the temperature dependence over the measured range. A first-order rate constant carries the unit s-1 because the rate of reaction is proportional to the concentration of the reactant; the constant itself is the proportionality factor at the stated temperature. At 300 K, $k$ was 0.037 s-1. At 340 K, $k$ was 2.581 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 90 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. The Arrhenius relation connects the rate constant to temperature through the activation energy, and the value at the higher temperature is reported on that basis rather than as a direct reading. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%. The triplicate measurements attach the same repeatability statement to each reported value; the spread is part of each result and not a separate finding. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. The measured range therefore ends at the higher temperature for a sampling reason: the sample changed while it was being taken, and a rate constant taken from a changed sample would not describe the reaction mixture. The two reported values, their common spread, and the stated end of the range are the complete result. The Arrhenius statement is the form in which the higher value is carried, and it is labelled as computed. The lower value stands as measured. Between them, the two values describe a reaction that runs faster at the higher temperature, and the description is confined to the interval the measurements cover. No value is carried beyond the upper temperature by the relation, because the sampling failure, not the relation, sets the end of the reported range.
